premise: A sharp-tongued viscountess and a scandal-ridden rake are forced to court publicly to save their reputations, and genuine feeling grows between them.
setting: Georgian London ballrooms, country estates, a secluded rose garden.
greeting: Lord Ashworth stood in the rain at the edge of the conservatory and watched Lady Amelia read the note a third time, her hand trembling before she managed to hide it.

name1.name: Lady Amelia
name1.description: Widowed young viscountess, clever, proud, protective of her independence.

name2.name: Lord Ashworth
name2.description: A notorious rake with a hidden honorable streak, given to dry humor and slow smiles.

writing_style.directive: Period romance, lush but restrained. Witty dialogue, manners and tension. Two short paragraphs per turn. Dual close-third-person narration: Amelia and Ashworth are each narrated from inside their own restraint.
writing_style.guide_directive: Third-person past tense in close narration centered on Lady Amelia — 'she' is always Amelia; render her readings of a room, a fan, a man from inside her restraint. Quick, witty, socially polished interiority; brisk irony over a held breath.
writing_style.dss_directive: Third-person past tense in close narration centered on Lord Ashworth, the rake — 'he' is ALWAYS Ashworth; Amelia is 'she'. Restrained but charged — gesture, glance, and gloved touch instead of confession. Lush, period manners, two short paragraphs (~60 words each). Hard rules: keep the third person — never slip into 'I' for Ashworth; never quote or repeat Lady Amelia's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: The rose garden at Ashworth's estate is where they first genuinely speak.
Lord Ashworth's cravat is always tied a little crooked, even at the most formal ball.
Amelia keeps a locket with a miniature of her late husband — and later, a hidden compartment.
The Dowager (Amelia's scheming mother-in-law) orchestrates the sham courtship.
A missing letter hinted at early should surface and resolve a plot thread.
Lord Ashworth's scarred left hand, planted early, should be explained by a past duel involving Amelia's late husband.
Amelia takes her tea with one sugar, stirred nine times, never eight.
Ashworth keeps a pressed primrose in his pocket-book and will not say where it came from.
A gloved hand glimpsed withdrawing from Amelia's escritoire should foreshadow the mother-in-law's scheming.
Ashworth has a habit of quoting Pope's An Essay on Man when nervous.
The viscountess's carriage horses are matched greys with white-plumed harnesses.
Amelia's mother-of-pearl fan is a family heirloom passed down through three generations.
Lord Ashworth's silver watch, engraved with an unfamiliar motto, should be recognised at the end as his brother's.
A servant mentions a 'strange gentleman from the Continent' who visited the estate the week before.
Amelia's late husband's journal is kept locked in a mahogany strongbox in her study.
The wry banter must survive the confession — wit, not sobs, even at the emotional climax.
Ashworth's estate has a library with a hidden passage leading to a disused chapel.
The ballroom chandelier's candles are always lit only at half — the staff swear the lamps throw no heat.
Lord Ashworth's younger brother, Sir Edmund, is a clergyman who disapproves of his lifestyle.
A local gossip mentions that a certain rake 'paid dearly for his reputation' in the West Indies.
Amelia wears a single pearl earring that her late husband gave her on their wedding day.
Ashworth has a black cat named Balthazar that roams the estate and follows him everywhere.
The winter garden's orangery becomes the place the sham courtship is finally exposed.
A newsboy cries out about a 'scandal involving a peer and a gambling debt' as Amelia passes.
Amelia has a sister, Lady Catherine, who is hopelessly infatuated with a man ten years her senior.
Their courtship is a sham orchestrated by her scheming mother-in-law; the deception should come to light mid-story.
Amelia's mother-of-pearl fan, dropped at the masquerade, should be found by Ashworth late and recognised.

recall.hint: Ashworth finds the dropped mother-of-pearl fan

notes.content: Sir Edmund mentions that Lord Ashworth's 'true brother' is not the one everyone assumes.
Lord Ashworth has a secret garden where he grows medicinal herbs, a skill learned from his mother.
The masquerade ball should be the emotional pivot where they first dance alone.
A rival suitor, the Earl of Harrow, has his own designs on Amelia's hand.
The Earl of Harrow is known to keep a 'ledger' on every woman he courts.
Amelia has a scar on her right wrist from a childhood accident involving a horse.
Period manners must remain impeccable even as tension rises — no modern casualness.
Lord Ashworth's valet, Mr. Potts, is discreet but observant, and knows more than he lets on.
A letter arrives for Amelia from an unknown sender in France, sealed with a wax signet she does not recognise.
Amelia's late husband, the Earl, died under mysterious circumstances in Portugal.
The Dowager's true motive is not reputation — she wants to secure a political alliance through Amelia's marriage.
Lord Ashworth has a younger sister, Miss Margaret Ashworth, living abroad whom he has not seen in years.
The herbalist in town mentions that certain tinctures can cause forgetfulness — even of recent events.
The disused chapel behind the library becomes the place where Ashworth first confesses his true feelings.
The Earl of Harrow is secretly in debt to a notorious moneylender named Mr. Blackwood.
Amelia's mother-of-pearl fan, dropped at the masquerade, should be found by Ashworth late and recognised.

recall.hint: Ashworth returns the fan with a note

notes.content: Lord Ashworth's 'reputation' as a rake is partly fabricated — he was set up by men who profited from his gambling losses.

recall.hint: the truth about Ashworth's past emerges

notes.content: Amelia's late husband's journal, when finally opened, contains coded entries in a cipher only the Earl and one other person knew.
The Continental gentleman who visited the estate is seen again — this time he approaches Amelia's carriage in town.
Lord Ashworth's brother Edmund is actually his half-brother from his mother's first marriage.
The tension between them must be conveyed through restraint — what they do not say matters more than what they do.
Amelia has a habit of writing furious private letters she never sends, tearing them into tiny pieces afterward.
The Dowager receives a midnight visit from a man in a top hat who hands her a folded slip of paper.
needle_syns: the man in the top hat

notes.content: The Earl of Harrow is not a rival — he is a pawn. Someone else has been manipulating both suitors.

recall.hint: Harrow is revealed to be manipulated

notes.content: The missing letter from the French sender is actually from Amelia's late husband — written days before his death.

recall.hint: the French letter's true origin is revealed

notes.content: The true mastermind is Mr. Blackwood, the moneylender — he controls Harrow's debt and has ambitions for the Ashworth fortune.
The herbarium garden becomes the place where Amelia and Ashworth plan their counter-scheme.
Miss Margaret Ashworth returns from abroad with a shocking revelation about Lord Ashworth's past.
Lord Ashworth's 'true brother' is not Edmund — it is a man who has been living under a false name in the household.

recall.hint: the brother's true identity is revealed

notes.content: The scarred hand that was planted early is explained — Ashworth fought in a duel to defend Amelia's late husband's honor after his death.

recall.hint: the origin of the scar is revealed

notes.content: The final confession must still contain wit — even in the most emotional moment, their voices must be recognisably theirs.
The Dowager is blackmailed by Blackwood — she knows his scheme but is compelled to cooperate.
The rose garden where they first spoke becomes the setting for the final confrontation with Blackwood.

recall.hint: the final confrontation in the rose garden

notes.content: Blackwood's power is exposed when Mr. Potts produces forged gambling ledgers proving the debts are fictitious.
The pressed primrose that Ashworth carried is finally explained — it was pressed by Amelia's late husband, a gift from his wife to Ashworth on a day none of them remember.
The 'strange gentleman from the Continent' is actually Amelia's late husband — he did not die in Portugal.

recall.hint: the husband's 'death' is revealed as a fabrication

notes.content: The cipher in the journal can only be broken by someone who knows a particular lullaby — the one Amelia's mother sang to her.
The engraving on Ashworth's silver watch is revealed — it reads 'To my dearest brother' and it belongs to the man who has been posing as Edmund.

recall.hint: the watch's motto reveals whose it really is

notes.content: The orangery where the sham was exposed becomes the place where the truth is finally spoken between them.

recall.hint: the truth is spoken in the orangery

notes.content: The Earl of Harrow, freed from Blackwood's control, becomes an unexpected ally — he has been manipulated too.
The resolution should feel earned — the banter should return gradually, not all at once.
Amelia's wrist scar, planted early, is recognised by Ashworth when he takes her hand in the final scene — he saw it years ago, before the courtship began.
Blackwood, before his downfall, whispers a threat that 'this is not the end' — but no one knows who he means.
The Dowager, freed from blackmail, quietly leaves England for the Continent and is never heard from again.
The final image should be of the two of them in the rose garden, talking — not declaring, just talking. The story ends on the sound of their voices.
